The conclusion is about that change, not about statistics that are out of date.\n\n**(D) Out of Scope.** Restrictions on advertising other products would not explain a drop in smoking.\n\n**(E) Correct.** Many other factors could have lowered adult smoking in the same decade. Without ruling them out, matching timing does not show the restrictions made a significant difference.\n\n## PT156-S2-Q11 | Flaw | D\n\n**Modelled on:** PT154-S1-Q12 (ad hominem), PT155-S1-Q20 (rebuttal flaws).\n\n> Professor Williams: Professor Thomas’s report characterizes our colleague Professor York as too flamboyant and confrontational in the classroom. But the argument given in this report sounds so much like the classic argument of the self-serving academic that one has to wonder if Professor Thomas simply is not the orator and entertainer Thomas would like to be, and so vents frustrations by condemning others—Professor York in particular.\n>\n> Professor Williams’s argument is flawed because it\n>\n> (A) confuses the distinction between being overly confrontational and engaging students by entertaining them\n> (B) presupposes the point it is attempting to establish\n> (C) mistakes Professor Thomas’s characterization of a view for an endorsement of that view\n> (D) attacks Professor Thomas personally rather than addressing Professor Thomas’s argument\n> (E) rejects the possibility that Professor York is in fact too confrontational.\n\nBank note: the stimulus contains an em dash in the original question text. It is quoted verbatim; the explanation text uses none.\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion (implied):** Professor Thomas's criticism of York should be doubted.\n\n**Evidence:** Thomas's argument sounds self-serving, so Thomas may be venting jealousy.\n\n**Evaluate:** Suppose Thomas really is jealous. Is York therefore not too confrontational? No. A jealous critic can still be right. Williams never looks at what Thomas actually said about York's teaching. The entire response is speculation about Thomas's motives.\n\n**Goal:** Expect the ad hominem answer.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Description.** Williams draws no distinction between confrontational and entertaining teaching. He talks about Thomas's motives.\n\n**(B) Bad Description.** The argument is weak, not circular. Williams does not assume Thomas is wrong in order to prove it.\n\n**(C) Bad Description.** Williams treats the report as Thomas's own view, which it is. There is no characterization mistaken for endorsement.\n\n**(D) Correct.** Williams attacks Thomas's possible jealousy and frustration rather than the report's reasoning. Even if Thomas is jealous, York might still be too confrontational.\n\n**(E) Bad Description.** This tempts because Williams clearly sides with York. But Williams never denies outright that York could be too confrontational. The flaw is *how* he resists the report: by attacking Thomas.\n\n## PT156-S4-Q14 | Flaw | B\n\n**Lower confidence: check the B note's paraphrase of the abstract key.**\n\n**Modelled on:** PT150-S2-Q4 (comparison across settings), PT107-S4-Q18 (match abstract wording).\n\n> Science writer: Scientists often accept a scientific argument largely for social reasons, such as the argument’s acceptance by other scientists or the prestige of the scientist making the argument. But this is not at all to the sciences’ detriment, for similar social factors strongly influence every human endeavor.\n>\n> The science writer’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it\n>\n> (A) takes for granted that the only legitimate reasons for accepting an argument are social reasons\n> (B) takes for granted that whether a behavior obstructs the achievement of a particular endeavor’s goals depends on the prevalence of comparable behaviors in other endeavors\n> (C) fails to consider the possibility that scientists who accept an argument largely for social reasons also generally consider relevant scientific evidence before accepting the argument\n> (D) fails to consider the possibility that many scientists are unaware that they usually accept scientific arguments largely for social reasons\n> (E) takes for granted that a behavior that is not detrimental to the sciences will not be detrimental to any other human endeavor\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Accepting arguments for social reasons does not harm the sciences.\n\n**Evidence:** Social factors strongly influence every human endeavor.\n\n**Evaluate:** \"Everyone does it\" is not \"it does no harm here.\" Cheating happens in many games; it still ruins chess. Science has a particular goal: finding out what is true. Accepting an argument because of who made it could get in the way of that goal no matter how common the habit is elsewhere. The writer moves from *widespread* to *harmless*.\n\n**Goal:** Look for the assumption that how common a behavior is elsewhere decides whether it hurts science.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Description.** The writer never says social reasons are the only legitimate ones. The writer only says relying on them does no harm.\n\n**(B) Correct.** Map the abstract wording. \"A behavior\" is accepting arguments for social reasons. \"A particular endeavor's goals\" are science's goals. \"Comparable behaviors in other endeavors\" is social influence on every human endeavor. The writer treats the fact that social influence is everywhere as settling whether it obstructs science. It does not.\n\n**(C) Strengthens, if anything.** If scientists also weigh the evidence, social reasons are less likely to harm science. That helps the writer rather than exposing a flaw.\n\n**(D) No Impact.** Whether scientists notice their social motives does not affect whether those motives harm science.\n\n**(E) Backwards.** The writer reasons from other endeavors to science, not from science to other endeavors. Nothing is concluded about whether the behavior harms anything else.\n\n## PT156-S4-Q16 | Flaw | D\n\n**Modelled on:** PT143-S3-Q18 (untriggered conditional), PT150-S2-Q4 (plan).\n\n> Manager: I plan to put together a successful marketing team by choosing highly skilled, independent workers who prefer not to work as part of a tightly knit group. This strategy is bound to succeed because recent research shows that when a common purpose is shared, the flexibility of loosely bound groups enables them to function better than tightly knit ones.\n>\n> The reasoning in the manager’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument\n>\n> (A) presumes that factors that are collectively sufficient for success are also individually necessary for success\n> (B) relies on research that has no apparent relevance to the manager’s proposed plan\n> (C) takes for granted that flexible teams always function significantly better than inflexible teams\n> (D) overlooks the possibility that people who prefer not to work in tightly knit groups may have difficulty committing to a common purpose\n> (E) confuses the goals that the manager is seeking to achieve with the goals that must be held in common by the members of the marketing team\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** The plan to hire independent workers who avoid tight groups is bound to succeed.\n\n**Evidence:** *When a common purpose is shared*, loose groups function better than tight ones.\n\n**Evaluate:** The research has a condition attached: a shared common purpose. The manager never shows his team will have one. Independent people who dislike tight groups might be exactly the people least likely to rally around a shared goal. If the condition fails, the research tells us nothing about how the team will do.\n\n**Goal:** Look for the untriggered condition: a common purpose.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Description.** The manager does not treat any factor as individually necessary. He relies on one research finding.\n\n**(B) Bad Description.** The research is relevant; it is about loose versus tight groups. The problem is that it applies only under a condition the manager never establishes.\n\n**(C) Too Strong.** The manager does not need flexible teams to be better *always*. His mistake is ignoring the research's own limit, not exaggerating its size.\n\n**(D) Correct.** The research applies only when a common purpose is shared. If independent workers who avoid tight groups struggle to commit to a common purpose, the finding does not apply to them, and \"bound to succeed\" collapses.\n\n**(E) Bad Description.** The manager does not mix up his own goals with the team's shared goals. He simply never shows there will be a shared goal.\n\n## PT156-S4-Q18 | Flaw | C\n\n**Modelled on:** PT141-S4-Q3 (anti-causal), PT120-S4-Q23 (plan vs status quo).\n\n> Land developer: In a certain nation, stringent regulations prevent private landowners from building on their land if any endangered species is present on it. These regulations make the presence of endangered species a severe financial liability for many landowners and thereby discourage the landowners from protecting the endangered species on their land. Therefore, endangered species would very likely not be harmed by removal of the regulations on land development.\n>\n> The reasoning in the land developer’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on which one of the following grounds?\n>\n> (A) It confuses a condition whose presence would be required in order for a certain result to be produced with a condition whose presence would be required to prevent that result from occurring.\n> (B) It justifies a claim containing a value judgment solely on the basis of factual claims that do not in themselves entail that value judgment.\n> (C) It unjustifiably overlooks the possibility that even if certain factors tend to produce a given effect, they may be likely to produce stronger countervailing effects as well.\n> (D) It fails to take into account the possibility that policies that are not in the interest of land developers may well be in the interest of landowners.\n> (E) It fails to account for potential reactions from private landowners who do not have any endangered species on their land.\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Removing the regulations would very likely not harm endangered species.\n\n**Evidence:** The regulations make endangered species a financial burden, which discourages landowners from protecting them.\n\n**Evaluate:** Grant the downside: the rules give landowners a reason not to protect species. But look at what the rules do directly. They stop building wherever endangered species live. That protects habitat. Remove the rules, and bulldozers can go in. A cast is uncomfortable and makes you skip exercise, but taking it off early can still do more harm than good. The developer counts the cost of the rules and forgets their main effect.\n\n**Goal:** Look for the net effect: the rules may protect species more than they discourage protection.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Description.** No condition for producing a result is confused with one for preventing it. The argument weighs effects, not conditions.\n\n**(B) Bad Description.** \"Would very likely not be harmed\" is a prediction, not a value judgment. The flaw is in the prediction.\n\n**(C) Correct.** The regulations tend to discourage landowners from protecting species. They also block construction on land where those species live, a stronger protective effect. The developer looks only at the first effect, so removing the rules could harm species overall.\n\n**(D) Out of Scope.** Developers' and landowners' interests do not decide whether species would be harmed.\n\n**(E) Out of Scope.** Landowners without endangered species are not affected by the rules in question, so their reactions do not bear on harm to species.\n\n## PT156-S4-Q24 | Parallel Flaw | C\n\nBank tag: Flaw. The stem asks for the argument whose flawed pattern most closely parallels this one, so this is drafted as Parallel Flaw.\n\n**Modelled on:** PT113-S2-Q3 (illegal negation), PT154-S1-Q9 (diagram each conditional).\n\n> A movie studio’s script readers discard all proposed scripts that are not submitted by agents, and they discard all scripts that are incorrectly formatted. So a script that is submitted by an agent and formatted correctly will not be discarded by the studio’s script readers.\n>\n> Which one of the following exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning that most closely parallels that in the argument above?\n>\n> (A) To be accepted, entries in the essay contest must be postmarked by the deadline and accompanied by a completed entry form. March 21 was the deadline. Thus, an entry that is accompanied by a completed entry form but postmarked March 22 will not be accepted.\n> (B) If your kitchen is well organized and you are a good cook, the meals you prepare will be delicious. The dinner Jon prepared last week was not at all tasty, so his kitchen must not be well organized.\n> (C) If Bob starts exercising daily, he will improve his fitness level. His fitness level will also improve if he quits smoking. So if he refuses to exercise and continues to smoke, his fitness level is not going to improve.\n> (D) The police are allowed to ticket any parked car that does not have a parking permit. They are also allowed to ticket any parked car whose parking permit has expired. Thus, the police are going to ticket Ruta’s car, for her parking permit has expired.\n> (E) Most dogs that have attended obedience classes respond correctly to basic commands, but only some are able to perform advanced tricks. Thus, any dog that has attended obedience classes and performs advanced tricks will be able to respond correctly to basic commands.\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Agent-submitted, correctly formatted scripts will not be discarded.\n\n**Evidence:** Not from an agent → discarded. Incorrectly formatted → discarded.\n\n**Evaluate:** Two separate triggers each lead to the same result. The argument negates both triggers and concludes the result will not happen. That is the illegal negation, twice. Readers could still discard a script for being too long or simply bad. Avoiding the two named reasons does not rule out every other reason.\n\n**Goal:** Find two sufficient conditions for one outcome, both negated, with the outcome denied.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Wrong Flaw.** Postmark and entry form are *requirements* (necessary conditions). Missing one means no acceptance. That reasoning is valid, so it cannot match a flawed argument.\n\n**(B) Wrong Flaw.** One combined rule (organized + good cook → delicious), then a failed result, then blame placed on one specific part. The contrapositive only gives \"not organized *or* not a good cook.\" That is a different error from negating two separate triggers.\n\n**(C) Correct.** Exercise → fitness improves. Quit smoking → fitness improves. Bob does neither, so his fitness will not improve. Same structure: two separate sufficient conditions, both absent, outcome denied. Bob could improve his fitness by eating better or sleeping more.\n\n**(D) Wrong Flaw.** The rules say the police are *allowed* to ticket. The conclusion says they *will*. The flaw is treating permission as certainty, not negating two conditions.\n\n**(E) Wrong Flaw.** This mixes \"most\" and \"some\" statements. The structure is quantifier-based and does not deny an outcome from two absent triggers.\n\n## PT156-S4-Q25 | Flaw | E\n\n**Modelled on:** PT155-S1-Q20 (rebuttal flaws), PT107-S4-Q18 (what the evidence does and does not show).\n\n> Translator: Dr. Abner, apparently scornful of my translation of an ancient poem on the grounds that it is inaccurate, says that my translation produces in most readers feelings other than those the original text was intended to produce. However, as Dr. Abner should realize, we do not know how people originally responded to the poem or how its author intended them to respond. So Dr. Abner’s criticism is unjustified.\n>\n> The translator’s argument is flawed in that it\n>\n> (A) fails to adequately address the possibility that the original poem had more than one author\n> (B) draws a conclusion purely on the basis of an appeal to popular opinion\n> (C) fails to adequately address the possibility that the original text was not intended to produce any particular feelings in the reader\n> (D) rejects an argument merely because of the circumstances of the person who offered it\n> (E) concludes that we cannot know that certain effects were not what the author intended merely because we do not know what specific effects the author did intend\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Dr. Abner's criticism is unjustified.\n\n**Evidence:** We do not know how the author intended readers to respond.\n\n**Evaluate:** Not knowing exactly what someone wanted does not mean we cannot know what they did *not* want. You may not know what birthday gift your friend hopes for, but you can be sure it is not a bag of wet sand. Abner only claims the translation produces feelings *other than* the intended ones. If the translation of a solemn funeral poem leaves readers laughing, we can be confident that is not what was intended, even without knowing the exact feeling the author aimed for.\n\n**Goal:** Look for the gap between \"we don't know what was intended\" and \"we can't know what wasn't intended.\"\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Out of Scope.** Multiple authors would not change the issue. The question is whether we can know some feelings were not intended.\n\n**(B) Bad Description.** The \"most readers\" claim is Abner's evidence about how the translation affects people. The translator does not appeal to popular opinion.\n\n**(C) Strengthens, if anything.** If the poem was not meant to produce any particular feelings, then the translation could hardly produce the \"wrong\" ones. That would help the translator, not expose a flaw.\n\n**(D) Not Ad Hominem.** \"As Dr. Abner should realize\" is a jab, but the translator rejects the criticism on the grounds of what we can know, not because of Abner's circumstances.\n\n**(E) Correct.** The translator moves from \"we don't know what feelings the author intended\" to \"we can't say the translation produces unintended feelings.\" Some effects can be ruled out even when the specific intended effect is unknown.\n\n## PT159-S1-Q19 | Flaw | A\n\n**Lower confidence: the A note relies on the correct circular answer being rare. Check that the explanation of the hidden premise is clear.**\n\n**Modelled on:** PT122-S2-Q23 (runner-up: the rare correct circular answer), PT113-S2-Q3 (test each answer against the argument's shape).\n\n> Company spokesperson: Although our products are the most expensive in our industry, they are also the best available. After all, consider any less expensive product made by one of our competitors. If it were as good as, or better than, our product, it would cost as much, or more.\n>\n> The reasoning in the company spokesperson’s argument is flawed in that the argument\n>\n> (A) contains a premise that presupposes the truth of the conclusion\n> (B) fails to make a needed distinction between the best product currently available and the best product that could be produced\n> (C) treats a cause of a product being the most expensive as an effect of its being the most expensive\n> (D) presumes that because something is true of each of a company’s products it is also true of the company as a whole\n> (E) bases a conclusion on claims that are inconsistent with each other\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Our products are the best available.\n\n**Evidence:** Any cheaper competing product, if it were as good or better, would cost as much or more.\n\n**Evaluate:** Why would a better product have to cost more? Only if price tracks quality, so that the more expensive product is the better one. But that is just another way of saying \"our expensive products are the best,\" which is the conclusion. The premise sneaks the conclusion in. Without already accepting that higher price means better quality, the premise gives us no reason to believe it.\n\n**Goal:** Expect the circular answer, which is rarely right but fits here.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.** The premise \"a product as good or better would cost as much or more\" holds only if price reflects quality. Grant that, and the most expensive product is automatically the best. So the premise assumes what the conclusion asserts. Circular answers are usually wrong on Flaw, which is what makes this one hard: here the premise really does depend on the conclusion.\n\n**(B) Out of Scope.** The conclusion is about products currently available. Whether a better product could be made does not matter.\n\n**(C) Bad Description.** The spokesperson never claims anything causes the high price or results from it. There is no causal claim to reverse.\n\n**(D) Bad Description.** The argument is about the company's products, not the company as a whole. No part-to-whole move appears.\n\n**(E) Contradiction.** The premise and conclusion fit together perfectly. That is the problem: they say the same thing. They are not in conflict.\n\n## PT159-S3-Q4 | Flaw | D\n\n**Modelled on:** PT154-S1-Q12 (ad hominem, \"you do it too\"), PT155-S1-Q20 (rebuttal flaws).\n\n> Toy manufacturer: Our competitors argue that we should withdraw our KlopperKidz toys from stores because several children have allegedly been injured by them, and manufacturers should voluntarily withdraw toys that can lead to injury. Their allegations, however, have not been proved. Furthermore, even if they were proved, our competitors’ argument would still not merit serious attention, because their toys have caused injuries, and they have not volunteered to withdraw them from stores.\n>\n> The toy manufacturer’s argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it\n>\n> (A) attempts to justify a conclusion by offering reasons that are mutually exclusive\n> (B) rejects an argument on the grounds that those making it have a vested interest in convincing people of the truth of the conclusion\n> (C) assumes that merely because something has not been proved to be true, it must therefore be false\n> (D) rejects an argument on the grounds that those making it have failed to abide by what the argument recommends\n> (E) takes a necessary condition for a toy's being unsafe to be a sufficient condition for its being unsafe\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** The competitors' argument does not merit serious attention.\n\n**Evidence:** The injury claims are unproven. And even if proved, the competitors have not withdrawn their own injury-causing toys.\n\n**Evaluate:** The second reason is the key one. The competitors fail to follow their own rule. Does that make the rule wrong? No. A parent who smokes can still be right that smoking is harmful. If KlopperKidz toys injure children, the competitors' hypocrisy does not make them any safer.\n\n**Goal:** Expect the \"you do it too\" ad hominem answer.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Description.** The two reasons are compatible. \"Not proved\" and \"even if proved, they are hypocrites\" can both be offered at once. \"Even if\" signals a fallback, not a contradiction.\n\n**(B) Wrong Flaw.** This is the other kind of ad hominem: attacking someone's motive. Competitors might gain if KlopperKidz is pulled, but the manufacturer never says so. The stated reason is that competitors do not follow their own advice, which is (D).\n\n**(C) Bad Description.** This tempts because the manufacturer says the allegations are not proved. But the manufacturer never concludes the toys are safe or the allegations false. The conclusion is that the argument does not merit attention.\n\n**(D) Correct.** The competitors have not withdrawn their own injury-causing toys, so the manufacturer dismisses their argument. Failing to follow a recommendation does not make the recommendation wrong. This is the \"you do it too\" flaw.\n\n**(E) Wrong Flaw.** No conditional about what makes a toy unsafe is reversed.\n\n## PT159-S3-Q15 | Flaw | A\n\n**Modelled on:** PT155-S1-Q20 (rebuttal misses the point), PT154-S2-Q12 (answer the actual position).\n\n> Schmidt: In enforcing township rules on how homeowners maintain their property, it is a mistake to encourage residents to report violations by their neighbors. Doing so engenders bad feelings among neighbors and leads to tips based on spite. Chandha: It’s not a mistake. Without rules on how homeowners maintain their property, a single homeowner could degrade the appearance of an entire neighborhood.\n>\n> Chandha’s response is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it\n>\n> (A) takes a criticism of the way in which certain rules are enforced to be a criticism of the rules themselves\n> (B) challenges the motivation behind Schmidt’s argument rather than Schmidt’s reasoning\n> (C) confuses a criticism of the consequences of having a set of rules with a criticism of the detailed provisions of the rules\n> (D) takes for granted that just because something is likely to happen on some occasions, it will always happen\n> (E) confuses the cause of bad feelings among neighbors with a consequence of bad feelings among neighbors\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Schmidt's claim:** In *enforcing* the rules, encouraging neighbors to report each other is a mistake.\n\n**Chandha's conclusion:** It is not a mistake.\n\n**Chandha's evidence:** Without the rules, one homeowner could ruin a neighborhood's appearance.\n\n**Evaluate:** Schmidt never said the township should drop the rules. Schmidt objected to one *way of enforcing* them. Chandha defends the rules' existence. Agree that speed limits are good; that does not mean paying neighbors to report each other's speeding is a good idea. Chandha answers a position Schmidt never took.\n\n**Goal:** Look for the shift from criticizing enforcement to defending the rules.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.** Schmidt criticizes a method of enforcement. Chandha responds as if Schmidt had criticized the rules themselves. Showing the rules are valuable does not show neighbor reporting is a good way to enforce them.\n\n**(B) Bad Description.** Chandha says nothing about why Schmidt holds the view. The response is about the rules' value.\n\n**(C) Bad Description.** Neither speaker discusses the rules' detailed provisions. Schmidt's complaint is about enforcement, which (A) captures.\n\n**(D) Bad Description.** Chandha does not reason from \"likely sometimes\" to \"always.\" \"Could degrade\" is a possibility.\n\n**(E) Bad Description.** Chandha never discusses bad feelings among neighbors at all, so there is no cause and effect to confuse.\n\n## PT159-S3-Q21 | Flaw | D\n\n**Modelled on:** PT154-S2-Q12 (false choice: a middle ground exists), PT120-S4-Q23 (plan with an extreme recommendation).\n\n> Sodium nitrate is frequently added to sausages to make them pink. However, sodium nitrate does not contribute to preventing spoilage of the meat, and excessive use of it increases the level of sodium in the sausages beyond what is necessary for good taste. Because consumption of an excessive level of sodium can lead to health problems, clearly sodium nitrate should never be added to sausages.\n>\n> The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on which one of the following grounds?\n>\n> (A) The argument makes a recommendation based on evidence from an insufficient sample.\n> (B) The argument does not address possible risks associated with the proposed recommendation.\n> (C) The argument presumes, without providing justification, that it is appropriate for the government to protect people from possible health threats without their consent.\n> (D) The argument does not provide sufficient justification for preferring the solution it recommends over more moderate alternatives.\n> (E) The argument does not distinguish adequately between medical and economic justifications for a policy.\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Sodium nitrate should *never* be added to sausages.\n\n**Evidence:** It does not prevent spoilage. *Excessive* use raises sodium too high, and excessive sodium can cause health problems.\n\n**Evaluate:** Every harm in the evidence comes from *excessive* use. What about a small amount, enough to make the sausage pink without pushing sodium too high? Nothing in the argument rules that out. Too much water can kill you; that is not a reason never to drink water. The author jumps from \"too much is bad\" to \"none at all.\"\n\n**Goal:** Look for the moderate alternative: use some, but not too much.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Bad Description.** There is no sample. The argument reasons from general facts about sodium nitrate and sodium.\n\n**(B) No Impact.** The obvious risk of dropping nitrate would be spoilage, and the argument already says nitrate does not prevent it. Losing the pink color is the only cost mentioned. The real gap is the leap from \"excessive\" to \"never.\"\n\n**(C) Out of Scope.** The government is never mentioned. The argument is a recommendation, not a policy about consent.\n\n**(D) Correct.** The evidence only shows that *excessive* use is a problem. Limiting the amount would address that problem and keep the color. The argument never explains why a total ban is better than moderation.\n\n**(E) Out of Scope.** No economic justification appears. The reasoning is entirely about spoilage, taste and health.\n\n## PT159-S3-Q23 | Flaw | C\n\n**Modelled on:** PT144-S3-Q15 (groups and overlap), PT148-S1-Q2 (numbers before the choices).\n\n> Principal: All of our school’s rural students participate in the school’s lunch program because they live too far away to go home for lunch, while roughly one half of their urban counterparts also take part in the program. Some participants in this program, including some of the school’s strongest academic achievers, also participate in extracurricular activities such as sports and drama. Therefore, we know that some of the participants in extracurricular activities are rural students and some are urban students.\n>\n> The reasoning in the principal’s argument is flawed because this argument\n>\n> (A) takes for granted that a greater number of strong academic achievers than those who are not strong academic achievers participate in extracurricular activities\n> (B) takes for granted that a greater number of rural students than urban students participate in extracurricular activities\n> (C) ignores the possibility that those who participate both in the lunch program and in extracurricular activities do not include both urban and rural students\n> (D) ignores the possibility that both rural and urban students have many other ways of occupying their time besides extracurricular activities\n> (E) at first uses the word “participate” in one sense and then illicitly allows the word’s meaning to change\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Some extracurricular participants are rural and some are urban.\n\n**Evidence:** The lunch program includes all rural students and about half of urban students. *Some* lunch participants do extracurriculars.\n\n**Evaluate:** \"Some\" can be very few. Picture 100 lunch participants: 60 rural, 40 urban. Ten of them do extracurriculars. Could all ten be rural? Yes. Could all ten be urban? Yes. The lunch program has both kinds of students, but the slice that does extracurriculars might come from only one kind.\n\n**Goal:** Look for the possibility that the overlap is all rural or all urban.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Out of Scope.** How many strong achievers versus others do extracurriculars has no bearing on whether both rural and urban students are among them.\n\n**(B) Not Assumed.** The principal claims only that *some* of each group participate, not that one group outnumbers the other.\n\n**(C) Correct.** The students who do both lunch and extracurriculars might all be rural, or all urban. The mix in the lunch program says nothing about the mix in that overlap, so the principal cannot conclude both groups are represented.\n\n**(D) Out of Scope.** Other ways of spending time do not affect whether some rural and some urban students do extracurriculars.\n\n**(E) Not Equivocation.** \"Participate\" means taking part in both uses. The meaning does not shift.\n\n## PT159-S3-Q25 | Flaw | E\n\n**Lower confidence: confirm that the E note's reading of \"have not accepted\" (withholding acceptance, not rejecting) is the intended contrast.**\n\n**Modelled on:** PT155-S1-Q20 (unproven vs proven false, modern version), PT103-S2-Q21 (absence of evidence).\n\n> Paleontologist: Most biologists accept that birds evolved from dinosaurs known as maniraptors. Some biologists have not accepted this theory, because the oldest known bird fossils predate the oldest known maniraptor fossils by several million years. This reasoning is misguided, however; the fact that no maniraptor fossils of a certain age have been discovered hardly rules out the possibility that such fossils exist.\n>\n> The paleontologist’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on which one of the following grounds?\n>\n> (A) It overlooks the possibility that even if a particular argument against a theory is misguided, that theory may nonetheless be untrue.\n> (B) It fails to address adequately the possibility that even if maniraptors existed before the first birds did, there may not be any maniraptor fossils older than the oldest known bird fossils.\n> (C) It takes for granted that if there are any maniraptor fossils older than the oldest known bird fossils, this itself proves that birds evolved from maniraptors.\n> (D) It overlooks the possibility that there may be substantial evidence that birds did not evolve from maniraptors, but that this evidence may be unrelated to the ages of any known or unknown bird and maniraptor fossils.\n> (E) It fails to address adequately the possibility that it can be reasonable to refuse to accept a theory solely on the grounds that the evidence yet discovered for the theory appears to be insufficient.\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Some biologists' position:** They have *not accepted* the theory, because no maniraptor fossils old enough have been found.\n\n**Paleontologist's conclusion:** That reasoning is misguided.\n\n**Paleontologist's evidence:** Not finding such fossils does not rule out that they exist.\n\n**Evaluate:** The skeptics never said older maniraptor fossils do not exist. They declined to accept the theory until the evidence supports it. The paleontologist answers a stronger claim: that the fossils cannot exist. A jury that says \"not proven\" is not saying \"innocent.\" Withholding belief because the evidence is thin can be perfectly reasonable even if more evidence might turn up later.\n\n**Goal:** Look for the point that refusing to accept a theory on thin evidence can be reasonable.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Not an Objection.** The paleontologist never says the theory is true because the skeptics' argument fails. He says only that their reasoning is misguided. So this does not catch any move he makes.\n\n**(B) Strengthens, if anything.** If older maniraptors could have lived without leaving older fossils, the missing fossils are even weaker evidence against the theory. That supports the paleontologist.\n\n**(C) Not Assumed.** The paleontologist does not claim older fossils would prove the theory. He only says their absence does not disprove it.\n\n**(D) Out of Scope.** The paleontologist addresses one piece of reasoning. Other evidence against the theory would not show his response to *that* reasoning is flawed.\n\n**(E) Correct.** The skeptics refuse to *accept* the theory because the evidence found so far looks insufficient. That can be reasonable even if the missing fossils might exist. The paleontologist treats their position as if it required proof that the fossils do not exist.\n"}

### What the best Paradox explanations do

- **They name the expectation and the kind of fix before the choices.** PT148-S3-Q11 says the known difference (surveys) cannot be the cause, so the answer must be a second difference between the groups. PT152-S4-Q23 says the answer must show how a few devices have a large effect.
- **They give two or three shapes the answer can take, then sort every choice into them.** PT139-S1-Q15 (trees, birds, or a coincident change) and PT148-S1-Q12 (could not eat, chose not to, ate and the herd grew anyway).
- **They use a single test that works on the next question.** "Something that changed" (PT154-S1-Q6); "is this a timeless rule?" (PT107-S4-Q19, PT113-S2-Q17); "does it separate the two groups?" (PT148-S4-Q3).
- **On math paradoxes they predict and do the numbers.** PT143-S1-Q19 (averages), PT140-S2-Q7 (cost shares), PT120-S4-Q1 (count vs per-item). Each says why math is the one place to predict.
- **On EXCEPT they show the three-and-one split.** PT113-S2-Q17 states it in the D note; PT120-S3-Q15 lists the routes up front; PT101-S3-Q14 uses a fill-in sentence frame for every choice.
- **They use the background fact as a weapon against traps.** PT120-S4-Q1 (A and D contradict "big films gross 2-3x cost"), PT140-S1-Q20 ("any answer about wool sales is doomed"), PT148-S1-Q12 (it is an island).
- **They separate "didn't decrease" from "increased".** PT139-S1-Q15 on A and B; PT152-S4-Q23 on apprehension rate vs theft rate. This precise distinction is what beats the top traps.
- **When the key does something unusual, they say so and teach it.** PT120-S1-Q6 (the answer can undercut the first fact); PT121-S4-Q19 ("explain all the data" means both facts).

### What the weaker Paradox candidates got wrong

- **Disowning the question.** PT149-S1-Q10 calls it "hot garbage" and tells students to ignore it existed. Disqualified.
- **Pasted wrong-answer notes, often on the most popular trap.** PT113-S2-Q17 (A, B, C identical, A at 13%), PT105-S1-Q25 (A, B, C open with the same paragraph; B at 20% gets one sentence).
- **The top trap gets one line.** PT106-S1-Q17 (B at 23% is one sentence), PT152-S1-Q13 (A note is one sentence), PT155-S1-Q3 (B and E thin).
- **Misreading a choice.** PT128-S2-Q19 argues B as if it said "most crimes ARE reported"; it says they are not.
- **Wrong sub-type or wrong family.** PT143-S1-Q21 has a Strengthen stem ("support the prediction"); PT106-S3-Q13 is "resolve a dispute in favor of one party" and calls answers "laughably weak".

### Fidelity problems found (Paradox shortlist)

- PT128-S2-Q19: B note misreads the choice ("If most crimes are reported"); the choice says most crimes are **not** reported. Correct note also uses a sexual-harassment example, which is a poor fit for student copy.
- PT149-S1-Q10: author disowns the question ("hot garbage", "ignore this question ever existed"). Disqualify.
- PT137-S4-Q3: Evaluate analogy is built on Logic Games practice. Conflicts with the no-LG rule for student copy; otherwise a decent explanation.
- PT143-S1-Q19: worked example moves from OKC to "Austin" mid-sentence.

STIM: Leatherbacks, the largest of the sea turtles, when subjected to the conditions of captivity, are susceptible to a wide variety of fatal diseases with which they would never come in contact if they lived in the wild. It is surprising, therefore, that the likelihood that a leatherback will reach its theoretical maximum life expectancy is about the same whether that animal is living in captivity or in the wild.
STEM: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?
## Given that
Captive leatherbacks are exposed to fatal diseases they'd never encounter in the wild.
## How can it be that

## Evaluate
We're told there's something worse / life-shortening about living in captivity.
So if max life expectancy is the same for captive vs. wild, then we either need to hear: - something good / life-elongating about captivity - something bad / life-shortening about the wild - these fatal diseases that become a risk on captivity are not actually shortening the lives of any leatherbacks
## Goal
I'd be looking for a distinction between captivity and the wild, something GOOD about captivity or BAD about the wild, when it comes to life span.

# Paradox explanations: batch 03, part A

Source: the bank on current main (`3fb8c77` and later, worktree `../ai-os-projects/lsatu-wt-bankfix-b02`, detached at origin/main) and the post-batch-02 database pull. Batch 03 is the first 40 Paradox and Paradox EXCEPT slots in gap-list order; all 40 are already in the database. This file holds the first 19. PT117-S3-Q2 (part B) has steps and needs notes only; every other slot needs steps and five notes.

Steps use the Paradox labels already in the database (Given that / How can it be that / Evaluate / Goal). `Modelled on` references are picks from `models/Paradox-Method.md`. Tags come from the existing Paradox vocabulary in `lr_answer_choices.tag`; "Helps Explain" marks the four working choices on EXCEPT and "helps least" questions. Quoted question text is inserted from the bank by script, whitespace normalized.

## PT102-S2-Q17 | Paradox | D

**Modelled on:** PT101-S3-Q14 (EXCEPT, one frame for every choice), PT148-S3-Q11 (explain a difference with a difference).

> Nicotine has long been known to cause heart attacks and high blood pressure. Yet a recent study has shown that the incidence of heart attacks and high blood pressure is significantly higher among cigarette smokers who do not chew tobacco than among nonsmokers exposed to an equal amount of nicotine through tobacco chewing.
>
> Which one of the following, if true, helps least to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
>
> (A) People who smoke but do not chew tobacco tend to exercise less than those who chew tobacco but do not smoke.
> (B) Chemicals other than nicotine present in chewing tobacco but not present in cigarette smoke mitigate the effects that nicotine has on the cardiovascular system.
> (C) People who chew tobacco but do not smoke tend to have healthier diets than those who smoke but do not chew tobacco.
> (D) Chemicals other than nicotine present in chewing tobacco but not present in cigarette smoke can cause cancer.
> (E) Chemicals other than nicotine present in cigarette smoke but not present in chewing tobacco raise blood pressure.

### Argument Breakdown

**Given that:** Nicotine causes heart attacks and high blood pressure, and the smokers and chewers in the study took in the same amount of nicotine.

**How can it be that:** Smokers who do not chew have significantly more heart attacks and high blood pressure than chewers who do not smoke?

**Evaluate:** Nicotine is equal, so it cannot be the difference. The answer has to be something else that separates the two groups: another ingredient in smoke that hurts the heart, something in chewing tobacco that protects it, or a lifestyle difference like diet or exercise. Run each choice through one frame: "Smokers have more heart trouble than chewers because..."

**Goal:** This is a "helps least" question. Four choices will name a heart-related difference between the groups. The answer will not.

### Choice Notes

**(A) Helps Explain.** Smokers exercise less. Less exercise is bad for the heart, so this is a non-nicotine difference that fits the frame.

## 2. What the best ones do

- **Decide link or defender out loud, then commit.** The Evaluate says which kind of argument this is. Abstract terms and conditionals point to a link; real-world, causal, plan and prediction arguments point to a defender. Then it builds the matching thing: a diagram (PT150-S2-Q12, PT148-S1-Q25) or "Given that ... how could we still argue that ...?" objections (PT153-S3-Q15, PT143-S3-Q25). Step labels stay Conclusion > Evidence > (Intermediate Conclusion) > Evaluate > Goal.
- **The Goal lists candidate answers, not the task.** The best Goals list two to four answers in the stimulus's own words, and one of them is the key or close to it: "the helmet is not more properly part of the heritage of the Italian people" (PT154-S4-Q4); "the drop in participation ... would not be the same across all demographic groups" (PT150-S3-Q7); "changing personal behavior would not lead to the government changing its policies" (PT146-S2-Q23).
- **Negation is written out as a sentence, then judged.** The pattern: "If we negate this ... [negated sentence in quotes, often 'Yo, author --' or 'Hey, author --']. Does that weaken? Yes, because ..." The note spells out the negation of quantifiers: some becomes none (PT127-S1-Q13), at least one becomes none (PT145-S4-Q26), a double negative becomes all (PT152-S2-Q23).
- **Rank the negations when two answers both hurt.** PT127-S1-Q13 (A vs C), PT148-S1-Q5 (A vs B), PT113-S3-Q14 (E vs B) and PT146-S2-Q23 (A vs C) all say the same thing: the correct answer is the one whose negation hurts most, and it does not need to destroy the argument (PT140-S3-Q19, PT127-S1-Q19).
- **Worked numbers and analogies carry the hard gaps.** Examples: gene 80 to 85 (PT122-S1-Q10), 2 s / 1 s / 4 s (PT143-S3-Q19), 35/35/30 (PT150-S3-Q7), a 0.5% rising chance (PT140-S2-Q6), $50,000 lotto (PT122-S1-Q10), Tom and the traveling team (PT143-S3-Q25).
- **Conditional answers get a diagram and a contrapositive, not a negation.** "When correct answers are conditional, they're usually written in contrapositive form" (PT148-S1-Q5, PT150-S2-Q12, PT147-S1-Q7). "Putting the Conclusion on the left side of the arrow is always wrong" (PT148-S1-Q25).
- **Rules for strength, stated once.** "If an answer is phrased very strongly, then negating it always gives a very weak idea" (PT146-S2-Q23). "Most" is almost always wrong unless the conclusion is about "most" (PT140-S2-Q6, PT154-S4-Q4). "Some" is lovably weak (PT152-S2-Q23).
- **Named traps with a one-line example.** Illegal opposite or "Flip a Fact" ("tall children love their moms" does not give "short children don't", PT119-S2-Q10). Only Thing Mentioned is not Only Thing (earrings, PT145-S4-Q26). Premise booster (PT118-S3-Q19). Inference instead of assumption (PT148-S1-Q17, A). Attacking a concession (PT147-S1-Q7, B).
- **Phrases worth reusing:** "the lovable ruling-out 'not / no'", "Whenever we're doing Necessary Assumption and we see an answer ruling out an idea with 'not', we slow down and negate it", "Which answer, when negated, most weakens", "a thought the author must have been having in order to arrive at her conclusion", "authors don't assume things that hurt their arguments".

## 3. What the weaker candidates got wrong

- **The author disowns the key or the question.** PT144-S4-Q20 calls the correct answer "very flawed" and "technically written wrong". PT109-S3-Q25 ("a surprising correct answer to me ... If I were hating on this answer") and PT152-S4-Q13 ("this answer seems to bother me") undercut the key. PT109-S4-Q16 calls it "a weird question".
- **The Goal predicts nothing, or the wrong gap.** PT144-S4-Q20 ("does not lend itself to an obvious prephrase"), PT143-S1-Q3 ("go to the answers a little fuzzy"), and PT139-S1-Q19 give generic shapes only. PT109-S4-Q16's Goal names a different assumption from the key.
- **Speculation from outside or from the author's own life.** PT147-S4-Q21 (natural selection vs a supernatural designer), PT119-S3-Q15 (the author's Twitter use; modern literature "probably more respectful of women and minorities"), PT119-S2-Q10 (asides on how residency really works; labeled as not needed, but they take space).
- **Politically loaded examples in a teaching brand.** PT145-S2-Q24 (gun control, abortion, party voters), plus a political slogan as the illegal-opposite example in PT145-S2-Q24 C, PT143-S1-Q3 C and PT127-S1-Q13 D. The logic is fine; the examples should be neutral (PT143-S1-Q3's blue and red M&Ms already is).
- **Thin notes on the top trap, or pasted openings.** PT104-S1-Q21 D (21%) gets two sentences. PT127-S1-Q19 A and B (21% and 9%) share one pasted diagram. PT151-S4-Q4 opens A, B and C with the same sentence. PT142-S4-Q4 A to C share a template. PT105-S2-Q20 gives the correct answer of an EXCEPT one line.

## PT119-S2-Q6 | Paradox | B

**Modelled on:** PT120-S4-Q1 (the answer beats the others, not perfection), PT152-S4-Q23 (attack the evidence directly).

> University budget committee: Athletes experience fewer injuries on artificial-turf athletic fields than on natural-grass fields. Additionally, natural-grass fields are more expensive to maintain than fields made of artificial turf. Nevertheless, this committee recommends replacing the university's current artificial-turf field with a natural-grass field.
>
> Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the committee's position?
>
> (A) The university's current artificial-turf athletic field has required extensive maintenance since its original installation.
> (B) Most injuries sustained on artificial-turf fields take longer to heal and require more expensive physical therapy than do injuries sustained on natural-grass fields.
> (C) It is difficult for spectators at athletic events to determine whether an athletic field is artificial turf or natural grass.
> (D) Maintaining artificial-turf fields involves the occasional replacement of damaged sections of turf, whereas natural-grass fields require daily watering and periodic fertilization.
> (E) Athletes who have spent most of their playing time on natural-grass fields generally prefer not to play on artificial-turf fields.

### Argument Breakdown

**Given that:** Artificial turf causes fewer injuries and costs less to maintain than grass.

**How can it be that:** The committee recommends replacing the turf with grass?

**Evaluate:** The committee's own evidence favors turf on both counts. To resolve this, find something that outweighs those advantages. The injury figure counts injuries, not how bad they are. If turf injuries are worse and cost more, fewer injuries might still be the worse deal.

**Goal:** Find a reason grass is better despite fewer injuries and lower maintenance on turf.

### Choice Notes

**(A) Too Weak.** The current turf has needed a lot of maintenance, but we already know grass costs more to maintain. This does not outweigh that.

**(B) Correct.** Turf injuries are fewer, but each one heals more slowly and needs more expensive therapy. That cost could outweigh the cheaper maintenance and make turf the more expensive field overall, which is the kind of reason a budget committee acts on.

**(C) No Impact.** Whether spectators can tell the difference does not affect injuries or cost.

**(D) No Impact.** This lists different maintenance tasks, but we already know grass is more expensive to maintain overall.

**(E) Out of Scope.** This is a *budget* committee, so player preference is not the kind of reason that drives its recommendation. And nothing says this university's athletes have played mostly on grass, so we do not even know the preference applies to them.

Source: the designated bank (`../ai-os-projects/lsatu-wt-glossary/public/data/`) and the 2026-10-01 post-batch-01 database pull. Batch 02 is every remaining slot tagged Flaw or Flawed Reasoning: 40 in all. This file holds the first 20 in gap-list order.

Slot states in this part: PT107-S3-Q7 needs only its missing C note (steps and four notes exist). PT120-S1-Q23 has steps and needs all five notes. PT120-S1-Q8 and the five PT121/PT122 slots are in the database with no explanation. The remaining 12 (PT127 onward) are not in the database at all; loading them will also insert the question and choices from the bank.
def parse_drafts():
    slots = {}
    for path in DRAFTS:
        text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        for sec in text.split("\n## ")[1:]:
            head = sec.split("\n", 1)[0]
            slot, qtype, key = [x.strip() for x in head.split("|")]
            steps, notes = [], {}
            bd = sec.split("### Argument Breakdown", 1)
            if len(bd) == 2:
                part = bd[1].split("### Choice Notes", 1)[0]
                for m in re.finditer(r"^\*\*(.+?):\*\* (.+?)(?=\n\n\*\*|\Z)", part.strip(), re.S | re.M):
                    steps.append((m.group(1).strip(), m.group(2).strip()))
            cn = sec.split("### Choice Notes", 1)[1]
            for m in re.finditer(r"^\*\*\(([A-E])\) (.+?)\.\*\* (.+?)(?=\n\n\*\*\(|\Z)", cn.strip(), re.S | re.M):
                notes[m.group(1)] = (m.group(2).strip(), m.group(3).strip())
            slots[slot] = dict(type=qtype, key=key, steps=steps, notes=notes)
    return slots

### Choice Notes

**(A) Irrelevant Comparison.** Comparing leatherbacks with other reptiles does not separate captivity from the wild.

**(B) Irrelevant Comparison.** Sea turtles living longer than other marine animals says nothing about captivity versus the wild.

These are the last 19 Paradox gaps. PT124-S2-Q1 is in the database with no explanation. Tags come from the existing Paradox vocabulary. Quoted question text is inserted from the bank by script.\n\n## PT124-S2-Q1 | Paradox | A\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that:** Toxaphene was banned in North America in the early 1980s and is now used only in a few other parts of the world.\n\n**How can it be that:** Lake Laberge, in Canada, has high levels of toxaphene today?\n\n**Evaluate:** Two ways the pesticide could be there. It could have arrived recently from somewhere it is still used, or it could be left over from before the ban. Either story resolves the puzzle.\n\n**Goal:** Find a source: old toxaphene that never went away, or new toxaphene arriving from elsewhere.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Correct.** Pesticide levels often stay high for decades after use ends. The ban was only a few decades ago, so the toxaphene in the lake can simply be left over from before it.\n\n**(B) No Impact.** Other pesticides in the water do not explain where the toxaphene came from.\n\n**(C) Deepens Paradox.** If toxic chemicals rarely travel far through the air, toxaphene from distant countries is less likely to reach the lake. This closes off one explanation.\n\n**(D) No Impact.** Manufacturers opposing the ban does not mean anyone kept using toxaphene after it.\n\n**(E) Out of Scope.** The puzzle is toxaphene in the lake's water. How easily it is detected in fish says nothing about why it is there.\n\n## PT127-S1-Q11 | Paradox | B\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that:** The more high-stress points a bridge has, the more likely it is to fracture.\n\n**How can it be that:** The fractures develop somewhere other than the high-stress points?\n\n**Evaluate:** Both facts have to fit. High-stress points must raise the risk of fracture, yet the break happens elsewhere. So the stress has to cause trouble somewhere else on the bridge.\n\n**Goal:** Find a way high-stress points lead to fractures at other points.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Irrelevant Comparison.** Other structures having the same pattern does not explain why it happens in bridges.\n\n**(B) Correct.** Builders reinforce the high-stress points, so those points hold. The stress moves to weaker parts of the bridge and causes the fracture there. More high-stress points means more stress moved around, and so a higher chance of fracture.\n\n**(C) Deepens Paradox.** If fracturing creates high-stress points, fractures and high-stress points should show up in the same place. That is the opposite of what we see.\n\n**(D) Half Scope.** This explains how fractures can happen without high-stress points, but not why more high-stress points still make a fracture more likely.\n\n**(E) Half Scope.** Bad construction explains why high-stress points and fractures go together. It does not explain why the fractures land somewhere else.\n\n## PT127-S1-Q24 | Paradox | C\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that:** Experts agree that stricter car safety requirements reduce accident rates.\n\n**How can it be that:** Places with stricter requirements have higher accident rates per kilometer driven?\n\n**Evaluate:** The comparison is between different places, and places differ in more than their rules. If the strict places are more dangerous to begin with, they can have higher accident rates even though the rules are helping.\n\n**Goal:** Find a reason the strict places would have more accidents anyway.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Half Scope.** Newer tires support the experts, but this does not explain why strict places still have more accidents.\n\n**(B) Opposite.** Overconfidence after inspection is a way the rules could *cause* accidents. That supports the evidence against the experts.\n\n**(C) Correct.** The strict places have far more congested, dangerous roads. They would have more accidents without the rules, so the rules can still be lowering a rate that starts higher.\n\n**(D) Too Weak.** Seat belts discouraging reckless driving \"for a few people\" supports the experts a little, but it does not explain the higher accident rate.\n\n**(E) No Impact.** The accident rate is per kilometer *driven*. Having more kilometers of road does not change that rate.\n\n## PT128-S2-Q4 | Paradox | B\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that:** The bats roost deep inside caves, where the temperature barely changes from night to night.\n\n**How can it be that:** Many more bats leave the caves on warm nights than on cool ones?\n\n**Evaluate:** It makes sense for bats to hunt on warm nights, since that is when insects are out. The puzzle is how they know it is warm outside when the cave feels the same. They need some other signal that tracks the outside temperature.\n\n**Goal:** Find a way bats inside the cave can tell what the weather is outside.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) No Impact.** Female bats catching more insects on warm nights does not explain how the bats know it is warm.\n\n**(B) Correct.** The bats can sense barometric pressure inside the cave, and that pressure moves with the temperature outside. That is their signal.\n\n**(C) Half Scope.** This is a reason to stay in on cool nights, but it does not explain how a bat in the cave can tell the night is cool.\n\n**(D) No Impact.** Eating more in spring and fall than in summer does not explain the difference between warm and cool nights.\n\n**(E) No Impact.** Knowing that more than half the bats left on most evenings says nothing about how they choose which nights.\n\n## PT134-S1-Q6 | Paradox | E\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that:** The climate factors that create tornadoes have not changed since 1953.\n\n**How can it be that:** The number of tornadoes *recorded* each year has more than tripled?\n\n**Evaluate:** Look at the word \"recorded.\" The number of tornadoes could stay the same while the number we notice and write down goes up. Better detection would resolve it.\n\n**Goal:** Find a reason more tornadoes are recorded without more tornadoes happening.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) No Impact.** Meteorologists understanding the factors better now does not change how many tornadoes are recorded.\n\n**(B) Deepens Paradox.** Stronger tornadoes suggest something about the climate has changed, which makes the meteorologists' claim harder to believe.\n\n**(C) No Impact.** A slow rise in the last five years does not explain the tripling since 1953.\n\n**(D) Out of Scope.** Property damage depends on how much property is in the way. It does not explain more recorded tornadoes.\n\n**(E) Correct.** Many more citizens now help detect tornadoes. More tornadoes get noticed and recorded, while the number actually forming stays the same.\n\n## PT134-S3-Q8 | Paradox | D\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that:** The highways with the most traffic tend to be the most congested.\n\n**How can it be that:** Those highways have the lowest rate of fatal accidents?\n\n**Evaluate:** You might expect more cars to mean more deadly crashes. But congestion also changes how people drive. If congestion keeps speeds low, and speed is what makes crashes deadly, the busiest roads could be the safest.\n\n**Goal:** Find something about congestion that makes fatal crashes less likely.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) No Impact.** Distraction causing accidents does not separate busy highways from quiet ones.\n\n**(B) Restates Paradox.** This says where the high fatal rates are instead of explaining why the busiest roads have low ones.\n\n**(C) No Impact.** Knowing that the drivers are commuters does not tell us why they have fewer fatal accidents.\n\n**(D) Correct.** Most serious accidents happen at high speed. Congested highways keep traffic slow, so they produce fewer of these deadly crashes.\n\n**(E) No Impact.** Busy highways \"do not always\" carry more trucks. This does not connect traffic to fatal accidents either way.\n\n## PT138-S2-Q3 | Paradox | B\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that:** Venus has a hot core and must expel its excess heat, as Earth does. Earth does it entirely through volcanos and fissures.\n\n**How can it be that:** Venus has no active volcanos and no fissures from moving plates?\n\n**Evaluate:** Earth's method is not the only possible one. If Venus has another way to release heat, the puzzle goes away.\n\n**Goal:** Find another way for Venus to get rid of its heat.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Half Scope.** Rock staying solid at high temperatures might explain why Venus has no volcanos. It does not explain where the heat goes.\n\n**(B) Correct.** Venus's surface is thin, so heat from inside radiates straight into space. That is a way out for the heat without volcanos or fissures.\n\n**(C) No Impact.** Bigger temperature swings inside Venus do not explain how it releases heat.\n\n**(D) Unclear Impact.** Surface movement \"somewhat like\" Earth's is not a way of releasing heat, and the stimulus already says Venus has no fissures from that movement.\n\n**(E) Deepens Paradox.** A hotter atmosphere would make it harder, not easier, for heat to escape.\n\n## PT138-S3-Q14 | Paradox | B\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that:** New recycling projects could greatly reduce the city's garbage, which is a serious environmental problem.\n\n**How can it be that:** The mayor says the projects would work against the goal of minimizing overall environmental damage?\n\n**Evaluate:** Look at the word \"overall.\" Recycling could help with garbage and still do more harm somewhere else. A hidden cost would resolve it.\n\n**Goal:** Find a way recycling causes more environmental harm than it prevents.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Opposite.** Recycling trucks polluting less than incineration makes recycling look *better*.\n\n**(B) Correct.** Recycling would cost so much that the city could not afford other projects that reduce pollution. The garbage problem shrinks, but the environment loses more overall.\n\n**(C) Opposite.** If the city has to burn its garbage, recycling would reduce burning. That makes recycling look better.\n\n**(D) Opposite.** More use of recycled materials in manufacturing is another benefit of recycling.\n\n**(E) Opposite.** Recyclers consuming less is another benefit.\n\n## PT138-S4-Q5 | Paradox | C\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that:** Country X has the lowest reported rate of disease P of any country.\n\n**How can it be that:** Residents of Country X reported to have it are much more likely to die from it than residents of any other country?\n\n**Evaluate:** Both numbers depend on which cases get *reported*. If Country X only diagnoses the worst cases, it would record few cases, and the ones it records would be the deadliest.\n\n**Goal:** Find a reason Country X records fewer and more severe cases.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) No Impact.** Some forms being more contagious does not explain the gap between low incidence and high deaths.\n\n**(B) Out of Scope.** The stimulus is about *residents* of Country X. Deaths among nonresidents do not explain it.\n\n**(C) Correct.** Country X seldom diagnoses the disease except in the most severe cases. Mild cases go uncounted, which keeps the reported rate low. The cases that are counted are the deadly ones, which drives up the death rate.\n\n**(D) No Impact.** Year-to-year swings in the number of cases affect every country and do not explain this gap.\n\n**(E) Out of Scope.** More potentially fatal illnesses in general says nothing about disease P.\n\n## PT146-S3-Q9 | Paradox | E\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that:** One advantage of word-of-mouth marketing is that consumers are less skeptical of it than of advertisements.\n\n**How can it be that:** The campaigns work better when the booster openly admits to being part of a marketing campaign?\n\n**Evaluate:** Admitting the affiliation should make people more skeptical. So the admission must bring a benefit that outweighs that cost.\n\n**Goal:** Find a benefit of admitting the affiliation.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) No Impact.** The kind of products sold this way does not explain why admitting the affiliation helps.\n\n**(B) Irrelevant Comparison.** This compares people who respond to mass-media ads, but it does not explain why the admission helps the campaign.\n\n**(C) No Impact.** How the boosters were recruited does not affect how consumers respond to them.\n\n**(D) Out of Scope.** Cost does not explain why one kind of word-of-mouth message succeeds more than another.\n\n**(E) Correct.** Admitting the affiliation leads to a more relaxed, in-depth conversation about the product. That benefit can outweigh any extra skepticism.\n\n## PT147-S4-Q1 | Paradox | D\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that:** Cool weather weakens muscle power in cold-blooded animals, and the chameleon's tongue retraction slows sharply in the cold.\n\n**How can it be that:** The chameleon's tongue extension barely slows in the cold?\n\n**Evaluate:** Cold weakens *muscles*. If extension does not depend on muscle power the way retraction does, the cold would not affect it the same way.\n\n**Goal:** Find a difference between how extension and retraction are powered.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) No Impact.** Animals being more active in warm weather does not explain why one tongue movement slows and the other does not.\n\n**(B) No Impact.** How far the tongue extends says nothing about how temperature affects it.\n\n**(C) No Impact.** Where the chameleons live does not explain the difference between extension and retraction.\n\n**(D) Correct.** Retraction runs on muscle, which the cold weakens. Extension runs on energy stored in an elastic sheath, so the cold does not slow it much.\n\n**(E) Irrelevant Comparison.** Comparing the chameleon's retraction muscles with other animals' says nothing about why extension holds up in the cold.\n\n## PT147-S4-Q3 | Paradox | D\n\n**Steps only.** The existing five notes stay as they are.\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that:** Patients in private rooms generally get fewer infections and shorter stays than patients in semiprivate rooms.\n\n**How can it be that:** Woodville's hospital has only semiprivate rooms, yet its infection rates and stays match nearby hospitals with mostly private rooms and very similar patients?\n\n**Evaluate:** The patients are similar, so look at how the rooms are used. A semiprivate room is built for two, but if Woodville often puts only one patient in it, its patients get the benefit of a private room.\n\n**Goal:** Find a difference between Woodville and the nearby hospitals that gives Woodville's patients the benefits of private rooms.\n\n## PT149-S4-Q1 | Paradox | C\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that:** The dentist says to brush after meals to remove sugars, because those sugars feed bacteria whose acid causes cavities.\n\n**How can it be that:** The dentist recommends chewing gum, even gum with sugar, to prevent cavities?\n\n**Evaluate:** Sugary gum adds sugar, which the dentist says is bad. So chewing must help in some other way that outweighs the sugar, ideally by fighting the acid or repairing the enamel.\n\n**Goal:** Find a cavity-fighting benefit of chewing gum.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Too Weak.** Gum has less sugar than a meal, but it still adds sugar. This makes the gum less harmful, not helpful.\n\n**(B) No Impact.** Decay being reversible if caught early does not explain why gum helps.\n\n**(C) Correct.** Chewing gum makes saliva, which reduces acid and helps rebuild enamel. That benefit outweighs the small amount of sugar.\n\n**(D) No Impact.** If sugar takes 24 hours to cause harm, brushing after every meal seems less urgent. That does not explain why gum would help.\n\n**(E) Out of Scope.** Healthy jaw muscles are not cavities.\n\n## PT152-S2-Q8 | Paradox | B\n\n**Steps only.** The existing five notes stay as they are.\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that:** Researchers expected the cuttlefish's startle display to scare off predators.\n\n**How can it be that:** Cuttlefish never use it on predators, only on small fish that do not prey on them?\n\n**Evaluate:** Scaring off a harmless fish has to get the cuttlefish something. One possibility is that the small fish cause a problem for the cuttlefish even though they do not eat it, such as drawing predators toward it.\n\n**Goal:** Find a way that scaring off small fish helps the cuttlefish.\n\n## PT154-S2-Q3 | Paradox | D\n\n**Steps only.** The existing five notes stay as they are.\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that:** Horses thrive in grasslands.\n\n**How can it be that:** The horse population peaked during a cold period 25,000 years ago, then dropped quickly once the climate warmed?\n\n**Evaluate:** Horses depend on grassland, so the climate has to be changing how much grassland there is. We tend to assume grass grows better in warmth, but the stimulus never says that. If grassland spreads in the cold and shrinks in the warmth, the timing fits.\n\n**Goal:** Find a link between cold periods and more grassland, and between warming and less.\n\n## PT159-S1-Q4 | Paradox | E\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that:** The decaffeination process does not seriously compromise coffee's taste.\n\n**How can it be that:** When decaf first came out, many drinkers said it tasted rather bad?\n\n**Evaluate:** If the process is not the problem, something else about early decaf must be. The beans used, or how it was made, could explain the bad taste.\n\n**Goal:** Find a cause of bad taste in early decaf other than the process.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) No Impact.** More people drinking decaf today does not explain why it tasted bad at first.\n\n**(B) No Impact.** Whether people would drink it does not explain how it tasted.\n\n**(C) Applies to Both.** Food affects the taste of all coffee, regular and decaf alike, so it cannot explain why decaf tasted worse.\n\n**(D) Out of Scope.** Price is not taste.\n\n**(E) Correct.** Processors used only low-quality beans for early decaf. The coffee tasted bad because of the beans, not the process.\n\n## PT159-S1-Q9 | Paradox | B\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Given that:** Car shoppers mainly look for the most reliable models.\n\n**How can it be that:** Some of the most reliable models sell poorly to the people who say they care most about reliability?\n\n**Evaluate:** Those shoppers want reliability, but they have to judge it somehow. If they judge it in a way that can be wrong, they may miss the cars that are actually reliable.\n\n**Goal:** Find a reason shoppers who want reliability fail to identify the reliable models.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Deepens Paradox.** If shoppers care more about reliability than fuel efficiency, it is even stranger that they skip the reliable cars.\n\n**(B) Correct.** Shoppers go by a model's reputation, and reputations can be out of date. Protein only starts the chain.\n\n## PT115-S2-Q17 | Necessary Assumption | B\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Producing more cars with right-side steering wheels would remove one obstacle to reducing the automotive trade imbalance.\n\n**Evidence:** The Japanese buy few North American cars. Fuel efficiency and reliability used to explain this, but North American cars now match Japanese ones on both. The Japanese drive on the left side of the road.\n\n**Evaluate:** The columnist assumes driving on the left matters to Japanese buyers. If left-side steering wheels don't put them off, switching sides removes nothing.\n\n**Goal:** A link: driving on the left makes the Japanese less inclined to buy cars with left-side steering wheels.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Not Necessary.** The argument relies on North American cars being equal *now*. It does not need them to keep improving.\n\n**(B) Correct.** Negate it: Japanese drivers *are* inclined to buy left-side-wheel cars even though they drive on the left. Then the steering wheel is no obstacle, and switching it removes nothing.\n\n**(C) Too Strong.** A legal requirement would make the point even stronger, but the argument only needs buyers to prefer right-side wheels.\n\n**(D) Too Strong.** Removing *one obstacle* does not require most Japanese buyers to prefer the North American model.\n\n**(E) Too Strong.** The argument does not claim this is the *only* way to reduce the imbalance.\n"}
