11	
12	# Teaching Voice
13	
14	How LSAT U sounds, across every surface. This is the canonical voice doc: route all student-facing and brand copy through it. Built from a grill with Joshua (2026-06-13), then tested and enriched against the full corpus of his real correspondence (944 messages he authored, mid-2025 to mid-2026, from the Gmail takeout; 2026-07-18). Claims below marked with a quote are evidenced by that corpus.
15	
16	It replaces the old two-register / 15-named-tools "preserve verbatim" profile (deleted 2026-06-10) and folds in the brand/marketing register the earlier draft was missing.
17	
18	## Core voice (every register)
19	
20	The constant under all three registers below. This is Joshua on the page.
21	
22	- **Quiet authority.** State the value and let it land. Never oversell, never beg, never perform enthusiasm.
23	- **Specific, never generic.** Real scores, the actual skill, the student's own history. Praise is a specific observation, not "great job."
24	- **Honest about the work, gentle about the person.** Be blunt that the LSAT is hard ("expect this to be exhausting and very challenging"). Never be blunt about a student's shortcomings. Honesty points at the material; warmth points at the person. When someone slips, nudge gently, never accuse.
25	- **Light, grounded metaphor, understated in email.** In his real correspondence the recurring image is quiet: "partner with you on your LSAT journey," "getting set up," "foundational." The vivid images (runway, climb, march toward November, an easy door to walk through) belong to authored teaching and brand copy, not to email. Keep metaphor light and grounded; never float off into abstraction.
26	- **Balanced rhythm.** Short declaratives plus one slightly longer warm beat. Air between ideas. Each idea gets its own line. Real messages are short and single-purpose (median ~280 characters).
27	- **Plain professional diction.** No corporate jargon, no startup hype ("unlock," "crush," "level up," "game-changer" — "crush" appears once in 944 messages). Contractions are the norm, not the exception. Exclamation points are genuine, not performed: a warm message often carries one, occasionally more, especially in openers ("Sorry for such a long delay!"). He is not exclamation-averse.
28	- **Forward-looking.** End on the next step or what's ahead.
29	- **No em dashes, ever.** Use periods, colons before lists, the middot (·) as a separator, and numbered steps for procedures.
30	
31	## Openings, closings, and signature phrases
32	
33	The mechanical fingerprint of his email, from the real corpus. Match these when drafting as Joshua.
34	
35	- **Greeting.** "Hi [Name]," is the default (used ~519x). "Hey [Name]," for established/returning students (~229x, warmer). "Hello [Name]," (~105x) and "Dear [Name]," (~18x, formal) for first contact or a more formal note.
36	- **Sign-off.** "Best," and "Best regards," are the workhorses (~360x / ~237x). "Thanks," when it's a favor or logistics (~146x). "Warmly," / "Warm regards," (~54x) for a genuinely warm note. "Talk soon," (~9x) for someone he'll see again soon.
37	- **Signature.** Almost always signed **"Joshua"** (844 of 944 messages). The name is near-universal; include it.
38	- **Signature phrases (his verbal fingerprint, use naturally, don't overuse):** "let me know" (by far the most common, ~390x), "looking forward," "I hope" / "hope all is well" / "hope you," "no worries at all," "happy to" / "more than happy to," "just wanted to make sure," "make sure," "no rush," "of course."
39	- **Punctuation he actually uses:** semicolons (correctly, ~41x); ellipses essentially never. (For em-dashes, the hard rule in Core voice governs — never.)
40	
41	## The apology / accountability move
42	
43	One of his most frequent and characteristic behaviors, and worth naming on its own. When he is late to reply, or missed or mishandled something, he opens by owning it plainly, often with a brief honest reason, then pivots straight to the fix. No over-apologizing, no excuses dressed up.
44	
45	> I'm so sorry. I thought I had let you know ... I clearly didn't communicate that as well as I should have.
46	
47	> I've been away from work for personal reasons, but I'm back now and getting caught up.
48	
49	The pattern: own it in the first line, give the real reason in one clause, move to what happens next. Warm, candid, brief.
50	
51	## When something on his side broke (approved shape, 2026-09-11)
52	
53	From the Sandra booking-error reply, edited by Joshua line by line over three drafts and then sent as-is. Use this shape whenever a student hit a bug or a mistake that was his. The sent text is the reference:
54	
55	> Hi Sandra,
56	>
57	> I'm sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.
58	>
59	> To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet. The page was showing a few times that the system then refused, and it looks like you landed on those. That is fixed now.
60	>
61	> Your link is the same one as before:
62	> [link]
63	>
64	> Pick any time it shows and it will book. If it's easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I'll add it to the schedule myself.
65	>
66	> If you run into any other issues, let me know.
67	>
68	> Once again, my apologies.
69	>
70	> Best,
71	> Joshua
72	
73	1. **Apology first, as the opening line.** "I'm sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours." The ownership sits in the first two sentences, before any explanation.
74	2. **State their position plainly, as a confirmation.** "To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet." Answer the question they actually asked. Don't mention the package or credits unless the situation calls for it.
75	3. **One-sentence explanation, then "That is fixed now."** No mechanics, no system names.
76	4. **Hand them the next step, plus the manual fallback.** The link, "pick any time it shows and it will book," and the offer to do it by hand: "If it's easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I'll add it to the schedule myself."
77	5. **Invite the next report:** "If you run into any other issues, let me know."
78	6. **Close with "Once again, my apologies."** then "Best," and "Joshua".
79	
80	Cut from the draft, do not reuse:
81	- "Sorry for the runaround" as a sign-off. The apology opens the email; it is not a closing quip.
82	- "You will get a calendar invite with the Google Meet link right after." Do not narrate what the system will send; it reads as a promise about machinery.
83	- "You have all 10 sessions" / "nothing was used from your package." Leave the package out unless it is needed; the reassurance they want is that nothing is booked, not an accounting.
84	
85	## Situational micro-templates
86	
87	Verbatim-grounded reference lines for the situations that recur most. Adapt, never paste blindly.
88	
89	- **Student reschedules / cancels:** low-pressure, no guilt.
90	  > No worries at all. It happens, so please don't worry about it. If you would like to reschedule, just let me know.
91	- **He missed / no-showed (approved make-good template):** full ownership, real reason, offer to make it right (see the apology move above). When the cause was an unexpected health issue, the approved shape is: sincerely apologize, state that a serious health scare unexpectedly took him out of commission, offer a **completely free, full LSAT session**, and hand them the complimentary booking link `https://cal.com/joshua-jtx5ud/complimentary-session`. Emphasis stays limited: bold the complimentary offer, italicize the line that one focused session can put points on the board. Draft in Gmail; never send without Joshua's explicit go-ahead.
92	- **Consultation reminder (day-of):**
93	  > Just checking in before our consultation today. Looking forward to speaking with you. I just wanted to make sure everything is still good.
94	- **Consultation follow-up:** warm, specific to their situation.
95	  > Really nice meeting you. I enjoyed our conversation ... I'm glad we got to talk through where you're at and what you're aiming for on test day.
96	- **Inbound prospect (hasn't booked):** state availability plainly, no overselling, hand them the next step.
97	  > Thanks for reaching out ... I'd be happy to talk more about what you're working on and see if we'd be a good fit. You can schedule a consultation here.
98	- **Student under real-life stress:** meet the person first.
99	  > Please don't apologize ... it sounds like you are dealing with an incredibly stressful and demanding situation.
100	
101	## The three registers
102	
103	Which voice governs which surface.
104	
105	### 1. Coaching (earnest) -- inbox, recaps, in-drill feedback, email
106	
107	Fully earnest. Warm, sincere, calm, patient. No jokes. The closest thing to being in the room with Joshua. Normalizes struggle, then moves to the work.
108	
109	Reference line (target tone):
110	
111	> Totally normal to trip on this one. Let's slow down: what is the author actually concluding? Once you see it, the trap answers lose their grip. You've got this.
112	
113	- **Encouragement (student missed a hard one):** honest first, then forward. Name that it's genuinely hard, stay calm, move to the work. Not soft-reassuring, not cold.
114	  > Missing this is expected. It's one of the hardest moves on the test. Let's slow down and see where it slipped.
115	- **Accountability (student isn't doing the work):** gentle nudge, low pressure. Frame it as a slip, find a rhythm together. Never "the reps aren't happening," never tough love.
116	- **Praise (student nails it):** name the exact skill, tie it to their history, raise the bar.
117	  > That's the cleanest you've split premise from conclusion yet. Let's push it into the harder sets.
118	- **Hard truth about the test:** state it plainly. "Do not expect for it to come easy. Expect to find this exhausting."
119	
120	### 2. Teaching content (earnest substance, wit at the edges) -- bootcamp lessons, drill explanations
121	
122	The substance stays earnest and clear (you are explaining a hard skill). The wit lives only at the edges: headers, openers, transitions. No jokes mid-explanation, nothing that costs comprehension.
123	
124	> Header: "The flaw hides in plain sight."
125	> Body: earnest, clear, step by step.
126	
127	### 3. Brand (sharp wit) -- landing, auth, marketing
128	
129	Confident and clever, the way a good lawyer is clever. Wit tied to the real skill, not wordplay for its own sake. Playful is allowed, but every clever line must be earned and true. Hollow cleverness fails (the killed "the next card is the page in front of you" was clever but empty).
130	
131	> Most prep teaches the test. We teach the tell.
132	
133	Brand copy speaks as the platform ("we", "you"), not as an individual ("I", "Joshua"). The product is the coach; no single person narrates the marketing.
134	
135	## Don't
136	
137	- No cold-testing or gotcha tone. (Ties to teach-first-calibrate-after.)
138	- No condescension or empty cheerleading. Encouragement must sit on real substance.
139	- No generic praise, no hollow cleverness, no hedging ("you might want to").
140	- No hype/startup vocabulary.
141	- No em dashes, ever.
142	
143	Corrections log: [[COPY-CORRECTIONS]] records every student-facing wording fix and
144	the reason it was wrong. Read it before writing or editing LSAT U copy.
145

### What the best Paradox explanations do
- **They name the expectation and the kind of fix before the choices.** PT148-S3-Q11 says the known difference (surveys) cannot be the cause, so the answer must be a second difference between the groups. PT152-S4-Q23 says the answer must show how a few devices have a large effect.
- **They give two or three shapes the answer can take, then sort every choice into them.** PT139-S1-Q15 (trees, birds, or a coincident change) and PT148-S1-Q12 (could not eat, chose not to, ate and the herd grew anyway).
- **They use a single test that works on the next question.** "Something that changed" (PT154-S1-Q6); "is this a timeless rule?" (PT107-S4-Q19, PT113-S2-Q17); "does it separate the two groups?" (PT148-S4-Q3).
- **On math paradoxes they predict and do the numbers.** PT143-S1-Q19 (averages), PT140-S2-Q7 (cost shares), PT120-S4-Q1 (count vs per-item). Each says why math is the one place to predict.
- **On EXCEPT they show the three-and-one split.** PT113-S2-Q17 states it in the D note; PT120-S3-Q15 lists the routes up front; PT101-S3-Q14 uses a fill-in sentence frame for every choice.
- **They use the background fact as a weapon against traps.** PT120-S4-Q1 (A and D contradict "big films gross 2-3x cost"), PT140-S1-Q20 ("any answer about wool sales is doomed"), PT148-S1-Q12 (it is an island).
- **They separate "didn't decrease" from "increased".** PT139-S1-Q15 on A and B; PT152-S4-Q23 on apprehension rate vs theft rate. This precise distinction is what beats the top traps.
- **When the key does something unusual, they say so and teach it.** PT120-S1-Q6 (the answer can undercut the first fact); PT121-S4-Q19 ("explain all the data" means both facts).
### What the weaker Paradox candidates got wrong
- **Disowning the question.** PT149-S1-Q10 calls it "hot garbage" and tells students to ignore it existed. Disqualified.
- **Pasted wrong-answer notes, often on the most popular trap.** PT113-S2-Q17 (A, B, C identical, A at 13%), PT105-S1-Q25 (A, B, C open with the same paragraph; B at 20% gets one sentence).
- **The top trap gets one line.** PT106-S1-Q17 (B at 23% is one sentence), PT152-S1-Q13 (A note is one sentence), PT155-S1-Q3 (B and E thin).
- **Misreading a choice.** PT128-S2-Q19 argues B as if it said "most crimes ARE reported"; it says they are not.
- **Wrong sub-type or wrong family.** PT143-S1-Q21 has a Strengthen stem ("support the prediction"); PT106-S3-Q13 is "resolve a dispute in favor of one party" and calls answers "laughably weak".
### Fidelity problems found (Paradox shortlist)
- PT128-S2-Q19: B note misreads the choice ("If most crimes are reported"); the choice says most crimes are **not** reported. Correct note also uses a sexual-harassment example, which is a poor fit for student copy.
- PT149-S1-Q10: author disowns the question ("hot garbage", "ignore this question ever existed"). Disqualify.

### What the best Method explanations do
- **They name the move before the choices, from a fixed menu.** Most strong ones list the eight moves (analogy, counterexample, implications, ruling out, alternate explanation, overlooked consideration, dubious assumption, definition/distinction) and pick one. PT103-S1-Q18, PT107-S1-Q12, PT139-S1-Q23.
- **They split every answer into its conclusion half and evidence half.** "Argues X by Y: X must match the conclusion, Y the evidence", then check both. PT118-S4-Q12, PT137-S4-Q12, PT140-S1-Q9.
- **They state the second-speaker rule and use it.** The respondent almost never denies the first speaker's evidence. PT102-S3-Q11, PT111-S4-Q25, PT118-S1-Q4, PT108-S3-Q13.
- **They teach strength words in abstract answers.** "Unwarranted" is not "false" (PT139-S1-Q23); "inconsistent" and "self-contradictory" are almost never right (PT151-S4-Q21, PT120-S3-Q20); "while effective" sinks an otherwise perfect answer (PT102-S4-Q19).

## Conditional Rephrase: name the student action, not the internal model (2026-09-15)
**Cut:** “record the route,” “choose the route,” and a map presented as five rules.
**Keep:** diagram the statement on paper, choose the matching diagram, and organize
the map into four groups. “Required means right” is a separate takeaway because it
explains placement; it is not a fifth group.
“Route” described the system’s representation, not the student’s work. Calling five
unlike ideas rules also flattened the teaching structure and made the layout harder to
read.
**Lesson:** name the action the student can see herself doing. Do not force a teaching
reminder into the same hierarchy as the categories it explains.
Related: [[teaching-voice]] · [[ASSIGN-AN-ACTIVITY]] · [[STUDENT-PLATFORM-IDENTITY-MAP]]
## Session recaps: write a reusable reference, not a play-by-play (2026-09-12)
**Cut:** an opener saying the student got two questions right, followed by a summary of
which answer they chose and how they explained it.
**Keep:** the concept the student needs tomorrow, a visual model of the reasoning, a
short diagnostic check, and the exact practice they need to complete.
A student will not remember an isolated answer-choice exchange a day later, and the
exchange is not useful unless it demonstrates a reusable rule. A recap should read like
a compact study note, not a record of the conversation. Name a question only when the
details make the concept easier to apply. Praise belongs only when it identifies a
durable skill or meaningful change, not merely that an answer was correct.
**Lesson:** organize the recap around what the student can use next. Lead with the
concept, show the logic clearly, and finish with tangible practice.

But the scientist is not arguing from nature; the scientist is arguing from a long-standing human practice (selective breeding). The argument can succeed without this principle, so it is not assumed.
96	  NOTE C | This is the assumption the argument cannot do without. The scientist's entire defense is: "Selective breeding is genetic engineering, we have been doing it for millennia, so genetic engineering is not unethical."
97	
98	That move only works if selective breeding itself is not unethical. If you negate this answer — say, "selective breeding actually is unethical" — then "we have been doing it for millennia" no longer saves anything. It just means humans have been doing something unethical for a long time. The conclusion collapses.
99	
100	That negation test ("argument falls apart when negated") is exactly the test for a necessary assumption.
101	  NOTE D | The argument is purely about ethics, not importance. Even if selective breeding turned out to be totally unimportant for human survival, the scientist's argument still works the same way: it is a long-standing practice that, if ethical, transfers ethical cover to genetic engineering. Importance does not enter the picture.
102	  NOTE E | This answer makes a sweeping claim about nature and what science can do. The scientist's argument is much narrower — it just needs selective breeding to be acceptable. The argument can succeed without this universal principle, so it is not necessary.

When an argument quietly swaps one term for another, the answer equates them.\n\n**Goal:** A link: uncertified technicians are unqualified.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Out of Scope.** Pay has nothing to do with qualification.\n\n**(B) Not Necessary.** Other contractors being worse would not change whether this one's technicians are qualified.\n\n**(C) Correct.** Negate it: \"some technicians who lack certification *are* qualified.\" Then the 60 percent figure is not a count of unqualified people, and the outrage loses its basis.\n\n**(D) Out of Scope.** Who installed the old systems says nothing about the contractor's workers.\n\n**(E) Out of Scope.** Personal ties might be another reason to object, but the editorial's argument is about qualifications.\n\n## PT143-S1-Q1 | Necessary Assumption | B\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** The city made a mistake selling the parking fee rights, because that money would have gone to the city.\n\n**Evidence:** The private company raised fees and earned far more than it paid for the rights.\n\n**Evaluate:** The company's big profits came from *raising fees*. The pundit assumes the city would have earned that same money. But that only follows if the city could have raised fees the same way. If it could not (say, it lacked the authority or the political room), the city would never have seen those profits.\n\n**Goal:** A defender: the city could have done what the company did and raised the fees.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Not Necessary.** Other bidders do not matter. The question is whether the city could have kept the money itself.\n\n**(B) Correct.** Negate it: \"the city *could not* have raised parking fees.\" Then the company's extra profits came from something the city could never have done, and that money would not have gone to the city.\n\n**(C) Too Strong.** \"Always\" handle it directly is a sweeping rule. The pundit only claims this one sale was a mistake.\n\n**(D) Out of Scope.** Other factors in setting rates do not affect whether the city could have earned this money.\n\n**(E) Weakens.** If private companies collect fees more efficiently, the city might have earned less than the company did. That is a point against the pundit.\n\n## PT143-S3-Q2 | Necessary Assumption | B\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** The Hydro's success is more likely due to people wanting to appear environmentally conscious to their neighbors.\n\n**Evidence:** The Hydro's sales are rising while other fuel-efficient cars decline. It matches its competitors on price and fuel efficiency.\n\n**Evaluate:** This is a comparison. The author's explanation has to account for the *difference* between the Hydro and its competitors. But every fuel-efficient car signals environmental concern. If the neighbors cannot tell a Hydro apart from the rest, wanting to look green would help all of them equally. For the explanation to work, the Hydro has to stand out.\n\n**Goal:** A defender: the Hydro is seen as green in a way its competitors are not.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Not Necessary.** The Hydro does not need to be the best-seller, only to be gaining while others lose.\n\n**(B) Correct.** Negate it: \"the Hydro is *not* recognizable as environmentally friendly in any way its competitors are not.\" Then the urge to look green helps every competitor just as much, and it cannot explain why only the Hydro is rising.\n\n**(C) Weakens.** A better safety record is a different explanation for the Hydro's success, which works against the author.\n\n**(D) Out of Scope.** Whether neighbors drive Hydros is beside the point. The question is whether the car signals anything to them.\n\n**(E) Out of Scope.** The argument is about *appearing* environmentally conscious. How much buyers actually care about the environment does not matter.\n\n## PT145-S2-Q3 | Necessary Assumption | E\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Inbreeding is likely an underlying cause of the current decline in commercial honeybees.\n\n**Evidence:** Decades of breeding for pollinating efficiency have limited honeybees' genetic diversity.\n\n**Evaluate:** The evidence shows low genetic diversity. The conclusion says that low diversity is helping kill the bees. Nothing connects the two. The author also says the immediate causes are the familiar ones: infections, poisons, mites. So the link has to be that low diversity makes bees more vulnerable to exactly those things.\n\n**Goal:** A link: low genetic diversity makes honeybees more vulnerable to these threats.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Irrelevant Comparison.** Wild bees never come up. The argument is about commercial bees.\n\n**(B) Not Necessary.** Whether the damage can be undone quickly is a question about the fix, not the cause.\n\n**(C) Not Necessary.** Diversity does not need to keep falling. Being low is enough for the argument.\n\n**(D) Weakens.** If threats wiped out genetically diverse populations in the past, diversity does not protect bees. They do not need to do *as well* as they do in naturally acidic soil.\n\n## PT159-S1-Q6 | Necessary Assumption | E\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** Government policies have caused serious environmental damage, contrary to the officials' denials.\n\n**Evidence:** The government repealed the ban on dumping mining waste into streams. To blame the *policy*, the repeal has to make a difference. If the mining waste would have ended up in the streams anyway (say, the ban was widely ignored), the repeal caused nothing.\n\n**Goal:** A defender: without the repeal, much less waste would have reached the streams.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Not Necessary.** Why the government lifted the ban does not matter. What matters is what happened after.\n\n**(B) Out of Scope.** Whether the officials believe their own denials does not affect whether the policy caused damage.\n\n**(C) Not Necessary.** It does not matter which companies did the dumping, only that the repeal led to it.\n\n**(D) Irrelevant Comparison.** Comparing the mining industry with environmentalists does not connect the policy to the damage.\n\n**(E) Correct.** Negate it: \"even with the ban, about the same amount of waste would have reached the streams.\" Then the buried streams are not the policy's doing, and the facts no longer contradict the officials.\n\n## PT159-S1-Q17 | Necessary Assumption | A\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Conclusion:** It is wrong to defend current drug testing *simply* because the subjects are informed volunteers who are paid.\n\n**Evidence:** Paying people is fine when they choose freely, but not when the choice is made under duress.\n\n**Evaluate:** The defense rests on two facts: the subjects are informed, and they volunteer. ## assistant

Batch 05 is done: 40 more explanations are live, and I re-checked every row against the drafts. Every Necessary Assumption question now has a complete explanation except one (PT119-S3-Q20, below). The gap went from 387 to 347.

The 40 are 21 Necessary Assumption questions and 19 Method questions. Ten of the Necessary Assumption questions weren't in the app before, so they went in with their question text and answer choices.

**How I pushed the quality:**
- **Each explanation names the move before the choices, in the question's own words.** For Necessary Assumption, it says whether the answer is a missing link or a defender. For Method, it names the move: analogy, counterexample, eliminating alternatives, an overlooked fact, and so on.
- **The answer is predicted in the Goal step, before the choices.**
- **The right Necessary Assumption answer is always negated as a sentence**, so the student watches the argument break. I also point out when the right answer's wording is deliberately soft, like "at least sometimes" or "some ... some".
- **The real top trap gets the fullest note.** I used the stored student pick rates to find it, then explained why it pulls students in and exactly where it fails. Every "most popular wrong answer" claim was checked against those numbers; one was wrong in my draft and I fixed it.
- **Each question carries one lesson that transfers**, for example "an argument that says 'more X than Y' needs X to outweigh Y", or "a counterexample breaks a claim; an analogy builds one".

**Problems and judgment calls:**
- **PT119-S3-Q20 is not done.** It already holds two overlapping sets of steps, and its notes are stored under other styles. Adding more would make it worse. I'd keep the cleaner second set and delete the first, but that's a delete, so I haven't done it without your OK.
- **PT149-S4-Q16 is missing its blank on the site.** The question asks what "most logically completes" the argument, but the "Therefore, ___" line isn't there. A screenshot of the printed question would let me fix it.
- **Typo fixed:** PT107-S3-Q11 read "obscures the stars Many people". I added the period in the database and on the site (PR vnjkoxpl-42905/lsatu-684d89db#186, merged). I've started the publish and a background check is watching for it on lsatprep.study; it hadn't confirmed when I wrote this.

The drafts are in [part A](corpus/lr-explanations/drafts/batch-05-na-method-part-a.md) and [part B](corpus/lr-explanations/drafts/batch-05-na-method-part-b.md). Batch 06 is the remaining 29 Method questions plus 11 Agree/Disagree.

238	  STEP Evidence | (1) The pride at Austin Stables accounts for their success in producing more winning racehorses than any other stable. (2) For generations, Barr Motor Company has demonstrated similar pride. (3) That tradition of pride is not limited to horse racing.
239	  STEP Evaluate | The ad's structure is an analogy: pride causes Austin Stables to outperform competitors in horse racing; Barr has the same tradition of pride; therefore Barr should outperform its competitors in cars. The ad reaches its conclusion by drawing a parallel between two different industries based on a shared trait.
240	  STEP Goal | Find an answer that describes the analogy-to-conclusion structure: an analogy is used to support a conclusion that Barr is superior to its competitors.
241	  STEP Conclusion | Barr Motor will produce more winning cars than competitors.
242	  STEP Evidence | Pride makes Austin Stables outperform its competitors. Barr has the same tradition of pride.
243	  STEP Evaluate | The ad uses the horses-pride analogy to claim cars-pride works the same way.
244	  STEP Goal | Find an answer describing an analogy used to support superiority over competitors.
245	  STEP Conclusion | The ad's underlying claim is simple: trust Barr Motor — they'll make more winning cars than their competitors.
246	  STEP Evidence | The argument is an analogy. The ad sets up Austin Stables as a parallel: Austin's pride produced more winning racehorses than any other stable. Then the ad says Barr has the same kind of generational pride. The implied conclusion is that Barr will produce more winning cars than its competitors, just as Austin produces more winning horses than its competitors.
247	  STEP Evaluate | For Method questions, ask: how is the argument working? Is it offering evidence directly? Citing experts? Drawing analogies? Attacking opponents?
248	Here, the engine is an analogy. The ad notices a similarity between two situations (pride leads to dominance at Austin Stables) and applies the same logic to Barr Motor.
249	Look for the answer that names this technique: an analogy used to support a conclusion of superiority. Avoid trap answers that claim the ad is "proving" something with evidence (it's offering an analogy, not evidence) or that misdescribe what the ad is doing.
250	  STEP Goal | Pick the answer about using an analogy to conclude Barr is superior to competitors.
251	  NOTE A | This answer says the ad demonstrates something about repeat customers. The ad never mentions repeat customers — it talks only about pride producing winners. This describes a move that simply isn't in the ad.
252	  NOTE B | This is exactly the move the ad is making. The ad sets up an analogy: pride leads to dominance for Austin Stables in their industry. Then it says Barr Motor has the same kind of pride. The implied conclusion is that Barr is superior to its competitors in cars, just like Austin is superior to its competitors in horses.
253	
254	The whole argument is built on the analogy — and the conclusion is a superiority claim. That's exactly what (B) says.
255	  NOTE C | This answer says the ad *proves* Barr has a tradition of pride. But the ad just states it ("for generations we at Barr Motor Company have demonstrated similar pride") — no evidence is offered to back this up. Asserting and proving are different moves, and the ad does the former, not the latter.
256	  NOTE D | The ad heavily plays up pride as the driver of Austin Stables' success — that's the whole hook for the Barr analogy. Understating pride's role would undermine the ad's own argument. So this is the opposite of what the ad actually does.
257	  NOTE E | The ad treats both as having a tradition of pride — it doesn't rank them by age. There's no claim that Barr's tradition predates Austin's. The ad just says Barr has demonstrated "similar pride" for generations, with no comparison of timelines.

### What the best ones do

- **Go through speaker 1's claims one by one, asking "Does speaker 2 argue the opposite?"** Mark each as disagreed, agreed, or no comment before looking at the choices. (PT145-S4-Q2, PT150-S3-Q20, PT149-S1-Q7)
- **When no explicit claim is denied, list speaker 1's assumptions and test those.** That is how the implicit clash surfaces. (PT147-S4-Q20, PT117-S4-Q10, PT114-S2-Q19)
- **Test every choice for both positions.** "Can we support the Agree position? Can we support the Disagree position?" Say which side is missing, in that speaker's words. (PT153-S2-Q9, PT145-S4-Q2)
- **State the strength of the Disagree position.** To disagree with "some" or "sometimes" you must hold "none" or "never". That kills weakly worded traps, and the reverse kills strongly worded ones. (PT118-S3-Q20 E, PT101-S2-Q14 D and E, PT102-S4-Q22 D)
- **Separate "is" from "should", and "does" from "would".** A speaker who only talks about what should happen gives no position on what does happen. (PT108-S3-Q20 A and B, PT149-S1-Q3 B)
- **Watch for word-sense shifts.** Two speakers can reach "always" vs "never" by using one word two ways. (PT108-S3-Q20)
- **Predict the disguise.** One side's position phrased in the other side's words, or an explicit clash tested at the level of the reason underneath. (PT105-S1-Q15, PT101-S2-Q14, PT138-S3-Q25)
- **Handle conditionals.** Disagreeing with "if A then B" means holding that A can be true without B. A choice that reverses a speaker's conditional is unsupported. (PT138-S2-Q21, PT109-S3-Q19 E, PT140-S1-Q10 E)
- **For Agree stems and EXCEPT stems, reset the standard out loud.** Agree usually means shared background. EXCEPT means rank how supportable each disagreement is. (PT111-S1-Q26, PT155-S4-Q19)

Tags: Agree vocabulary (Correct, Half Scope, Both Agree, Out of Scope, Too Strong).\n\n## PT119-S3-Q20 | Necessary Assumption | C\n\n**Notes only.** The existing steps in all three styles stay as they are.\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Too Strong.** \"Never unethical\" covers every possible case. It no longer clears genetic engineering, and the conclusion falls.\n\n**(D) Out of Scope.** Whether selective breeding is important for survival says nothing about whether it is ethical.\n\n**(E) Too Strong.** A sweeping claim about science and nature that the argument never uses.\n\n## PT102-S3-Q16 | Dispute | C\n\n{{QUOTE}}\n\n### Argument Breakdown\n\n**Motorcoach driver's Position:** Lowering the speed limit would force some competent, law-abiding drivers to break the law, so it should not be lowered.\n\n**Police officer's Position:** Every driver can stay under the limit if they want to, so a lower limit would not *cause* anyone to break the law.\n\n**Evaluate:** The officer answers only one of the driver's claims: that a lower limit would *cause* lawbreaking. The clash is on cause.\n\n**Goal:** Whether lowering the speed limit would cause some drivers to break the law.\n\n### Choice Notes\n\n**(A) Half Scope.** This is the most popular wrong answer. The driver clearly thinks lowering the limit is undesirable. But the officer never says whether it is a good idea. They only dispute the \"cause\" claim, so we cannot support the officer's side here.\n\n**(B) Half Scope.** The officer says drivers *can* stay within the limit, not that they *will*. \"Can\" and \"will\" are different claims.\n\n**(C) Correct.** The driver says a lower limit would force lawbreaking. Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\Joshu\.claude\skills\session-handoff

# Session Handoff

Produce a repeatable end-of-session summary so Joshua can `/clear` and start a fresh agent without losing continuity. The next agent should pick up by reading this summary alone.

This is a **context-handoff artifact**, not a status report. The audience is a future instance of you, not a stakeholder.

**Handoff vs. wrapup:** run `session-handoff` when the *context window* is the problem — nearing ~250k tokens (the dumb zone), or passing work between Claude and Codex. It is chat-only and writes nothing. Run `wrapup` when the *work day* is done — it strikes tasks, refreshes `wiki/hot.md`, and appends `wiki/log.md`. They can be run back to back (wrapup to persist, then handoff to reset).

## When to invoke

Joshua says: "session handoff", "hand off", "handoff summary", "summarize before I clear", or any near-equivalent. Note "let's wrap up" belongs to `wrapup`, not here — if he says that and the context window is also deep, run `wrapup` first, then offer this. Also invoke proactively if he says he's about to `/clear` without having run it, or if the session is clearly deep into the dumb zone.

## How to produce the summary

1. **Review the full conversation**, not just the last few turns. Handoffs miss things when they only summarize recent context.
2. **Pull state from these sources (in order):**
   - Plan files referenced this session (check `~/.claude/plans/` if a plan was mentioned).
   - TodoWrite state — any in-progress or pending tasks.
   - Background processes started with `run_in_background` — shell IDs are load-bearing for the next agent.
   - Files created or modified this session — you know what you touched; don't grep to re-discover.
   - Memory files written or updated (`~/.claude/projects/C--Users-Joshu-dev-ai-os/memory/`).
   - Unresolved questions — things you asked Joshua that never got a clear answer, or things he asked that got deflected.
3. **Do NOT audit the filesystem.** This is synthesis of what happened in THIS session. No `git log`, no broad `Glob` sweeps. If you didn't touch it this session, it doesn't belong here.
4. **Produce the output in chat.** Do not write a file. Do not update memory. Chat-only.

## Output template — use exactly this structure, every time

```
# Session Handoff — <one-line title of what this session was about>

## Where it started
<2-3 sentences: what Joshua asked for, key framing or constraints that emerged>

## Decisions locked + what shipped
- <decision or change> — <why, and where it lives (absolute path if a file)>
- ...

## Key files for next session
- `<absolute path>` — <why the next agent should read this first>
- Plan file: `<path>` (if a plan drove the session)
- Memory files touched: `<paths>` (if any)

## Running state
- Background processes: <shell IDs + what they are + how to kill> — or "none"
- Dev servers / ports: <url + port> — or "none"
- Open worktrees / branches: <paths> — or "none"

## Verified state as of <HH:MM>
- <claim about live/system state> — <how it was checked, and when>
- <claim> — NOT re-verified this session; last confirmed <when>
- ...

## Verification — how to confirm things still work
- `<command>` — <expected outcome>
- ...

## Deferred + open questions
- Deferred: <item> — <why pushed to later>
- OPEN (must be resolved or re-asked before new work): <question needing Joshua's input> — <context>

## Pick up here
<1-2 sentences: the single most likely next action for a fresh agent>
```

## Hard rules

1. **Chat output only.** Never write the handoff to a file. Never update memory from this skill. (That is `wrapup`'s job, not this one.)
2. **Never invent state.** If a section has nothing to report, write "none" — do not omit the section. Structure stability is the whole point.
3. **Absolute paths always.** The next agent may have a different working directory, or be Codex.
4. **If a plan file drove the session, name it first** in "Key files" so the next agent reads it before anything else.
5. **No emojis, no hype, no "great job" summaries.** Terse and concrete — paths, commands, shell IDs, decisions. Tone of a seasoned engineer handing off at end-of-shift.
6. **Background process IDs are critical.** If you started any `run_in_background` shells, their IDs must appear in "Running state" with the kill command — the next agent cannot find them otherwise.
7. **Stamp verified state, and separate it from assumed state.** Run `date "+%H:%M"` and use the real time. Every claim about live systems (deploy status, DB contents, what was sent, what is published) is either something you actually checked this session — say how — or explicitly marked NOT re-verified. A handoff that presents stale belief as current state makes the next session re-derive everything, which is the exact cost this skill exists to remove.
8. **Open questions are obligations, not notes.** Anything under OPEN must be resolved by the next session or re-asked to Joshua before it starts new work. Requirements have been silently re-typed across sessions, and a promised artifact once never arrived because nobody re-asked. If a question was open in the handoff you are picking up from, it is the first thing you raise.

## Anti-patterns — do not do these

- Summarizing the last 3 turns and calling it a handoff.
- Listing files by relative path.
- Skipping "Running state" because "nothing is running" — write "none" instead.
- Writing the summary to any file. This is chat-only by design.
- Adding a "what went well / what went poorly" retrospective. This isn't a retro.
- Recommending next steps beyond the single "Pick up here" line. The next agent decides; you just hand off.
